title: New Hampshire Employers Warn Trump Immigration Policies Risk Turning Away Needed Workers
excerpt: Business leaders in one of America's oldest states say visa delays, enforcement fears and a $100,000 H-1B payment are deepening shortages in manufacturing, healthcare and tech — sectors that rely on Indian and Asian workers.
body:
• New Hampshire business leaders say federal immigration enforcement, visa delays and a $100,000 H-1B payment are making it harder to fill jobs in manufacturing, healthcare and technology.
  • Immigrants are 7.1% of New Hampshire's population but 8.3% of its labour force, with higher shares in manufacturing (12.5%) and professional services (9.6%), according to figures cited in the reporting.
  • Healthcare staffing firms say nurse arrivals through immigration have fallen from 250-300 a week to about 100, while 60,000 to 80,000 registered nurse posts went unfilled in 2025.
  • For Indian and other foreign professionals: new H-1B petitions for workers outside the US filed on or after September 21, 2025 generally require the $100,000 payment unless a rare national-interest exception is granted — check the USCIS rules before filing.

Business leaders in New Hampshire are warning that the Trump administration's immigration policies risk turning away foreign workers the state cannot replace, as an ageing population and low birthrates leave employers short of staff in factories, hospitals and technology firms.

The argument, reported by the New Hampshire Union Leader and Business NH Magazine, is not abstract. Tony Fernandez, president of the NH Manufacturing Extension Partnership, said Indian and Asian immigration is essential in the state's tech and life sciences manufacturing sectors.

"In a state with one of the oldest populations in the country and persistently low birthrates, immigrants aren't just helpful, they're essential."

— Tony Fernandez, President, NH Manufacturing Extension Partnership

A workforce that depends on migration

Between 2020 and 2024, New Hampshire's population grew despite recording more deaths than births, according to a Carsey School of Public Policy study cited in the reporting. That growth came from migration, including immigration. Immigrants make up about 7.1% of the population but 8.3% of the labour force, according to the American Immigration Council.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2113235753811448301

The concentration is higher in the sectors struggling most to hire. Immigrants account for 12.5% of manufacturing workers, 9.6% of workers in professional, scientific and waste services, and 7.8% in healthcare and social assistance. They are also more likely to hold an advanced qualification: 24.3% of immigrants and naturalised citizens in the state hold a graduate or professional degree, compared with 15.5% of US-born residents, according to the NH Economic and Labor Market Information Bureau.

Michael Skelton, president and CEO of the Business and Industry Association, put the imbalance plainly: "We don't have enough workers to fill all the available job opportunities in the state, across several different industry sectors. Immigration has to be part of the solution to ensure we have the talent and workforce to compete nationally and globally."

Healthcare feels the squeeze first

Healthcare shows the pressure most clearly. Greg Henrichon, executive vice president of Manchester-based Core Medical Group, a national healthcare staffing agency, said 60,000 to 80,000 registered nurse positions went unfilled in 2025 and that the gap could reach 250,000 in 10 years. He said the flow of nurses arriving through immigration channels has fallen from 250 to 300 a week to closer to 100.

Henrichon pointed to two specific bottlenecks. H-1B processing that once averaged about six months now routinely stretches to nearly two years, he said, leaving hospitals unable to fill roles for doctors, nurses, physician assistants, physical therapists and medical technologists. And the new $100,000 H-1B payment, he argued, is prohibitive for community hospitals, safety-net institutions and rural health systems that cannot absorb that charge for each hire.

Under the USCIS H-1B specialty occupations rules, the September 19, 2025 presidential proclamation requires the additional $100,000 payment for certain petitions filed at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern on September 21, 2025, on behalf of beneficiaries outside the United States who do not hold a valid H-1B visa. Petitions filed without proof of payment or a Secretary of Homeland Security exception will be denied, USCIS says. Exceptions are described as extraordinarily rare and require a finding that the worker's presence is in the national interest and no American worker is available.

Delays beyond the workplace

Attorneys in the state describe a system falling behind its own timelines. Family-based petitions now take nearly a year to process, up from less than five months a decade ago, according to the reporting, while asylum and refugee cases often take more than two years. In December 2025, the administration halted green card applications from nationals of 19 countries already facing restrictions, according to a USCIS memo cited in the reporting.

Employers must still complete the Department of Labor stage before a USCIS petition: the Department of Labor H-1B programme page explains that a certified Labor Condition Application is required for specialty occupations, which are capped at 65,000 visas a year plus 20,000 under the advanced degree exemption.

The strain is not limited to large employers. Landscaping and seasonal firms described workers carrying extra identification and fearing stops even when fully documented, after raids shut Massachusetts landscaping companies overnight. Refugee service groups in Concord reported spouses stuck overseas with no reunification timeline.

What to watch

No change in federal policy has been announced in response to the New Hampshire warnings. For employers and Indian professionals considering a move, the practical position today is longer timelines, higher costs for new overseas H-1B hires, and a narrow exception route. Business groups say clarity itself would help: the sooner policy stabilises, Skelton argued, the better positioned employers will be to plan hiring.
